evidence: Cic. Fam. 4.12.1: nōn jūcundissimum mē nūntium vōbīs allātūrum
terms.comment: Also the messenger who brings it. A phone message is nūntius tēlephōnicus (M-O s.v. telephone message); Traupman gives the word among his computer terms too.

terms.gloss: a message given to someone to deliver; instructions
terms.grammar: noun, second declension; usually plural, mandāta
evidence: Cic. Att. 7.14.1: L. Caesar mandāta Caesaris dētulit ad Pompejum
Caes. BG 1.35.1: lēgātōs cum hīs mandātīs mittit
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “a charge, order, commission”; mandāta dare, dēferre, to give, to deliver a message.

evidence: Cic. Att. 11.24.4: nē per litterās quidem aut per nūntium

phrases.latin: etsī sciō nōn jūcundissimum mē nūntium vōbīs allātūrum, tamen … vīsum est faciendum, quōquō modō rēs sē habēret, vōs certiōrēs facere.
phrases.english: Although I know that the message I bring you is far from welcome, … I thought I should let you know how things stand, whatever they are.

phrases.latin: Inest lepōs in nūntiō tuō magnus, mea Ampelisca.
phrases.english: There’s great charm in your news, my Ampelisca.

sources: Lewis & Short: nuntius · Lewis & Short: mandatum · Lewis & Short: littera
